text: The South Carolina Republican Party (SCGOP) is the state affiliate of the national Republican Party and one of two major political parties in South Carolina, the other being the South Carolina Democratic Party, and is the dominant party. Incumbent governor Henry McMaster, as well as U.S. Senators Tim Scott and Lindsey Graham, are members of the Republican Party. Graham has served since January 3, 2003, after being elected in 2002 and re-elected in 2008, 2014, and 2020; Tim Scott was appointed in 2013 by then-governor Nikki Haley, who is also a Republican. Since 2003, every governor of South Carolina has been a Republican. Republicans hold a supermajority in both the South Carolina Senate and South Carolina House of Representatives. In 2020, District 1, previously represented by Democrat Joe Cunningham, was won by Republican Nancy Mace; the party now represents six out of seven of the state's congressional districts. In 1868, legislation prohibiting racial discrimination in public accommodations was passed by the state house but failed in the state senate. Benjamin F. Randolph, a state legislator and chair of the party, and another legislator were murdered that year. The Republican Party of the United States was founded in the 1850s in response to political tensions over slavery, with the goal of abolishing slavery and preserving the national government over state governments. This led to increasing divisions between northern and southern states, culminating in South Carolina's secession in 1860, followed by the American Civil War beginning in 1861, which ended in 1865 with Union victory. Following the war, the southern states, including South Carolina, were reintegrated into the Union during the Reconstruction Era, during which Northern Republicans and freed slaves controlled state politics, while Confederates were temporarily disenfranchised. The Republican Party of South Carolina was established during this period and dominated state politics throughout Reconstruction. Democrats responded with increasing violence and fraud at elections from 1868 onward, including the rise of the paramilitary Red Shirts in 1874, which disrupted Republican meetings, suppressed Black voting, and sought to restore Democratic control, especially in counties where Black populations were a minority. White Democrats led by Wade Hampton won the governorship and control of the state legislature in 1876 and dominated state government for decades, controlling most gubernatorial and national office candidates. Freedmen were still able to elect Republicans to local offices in some counties, allowing them a role in daily governance. After a brief coalition between Republicans and Populists in the late 19th century, the South Carolina legislature passed a constitution in 1895 that disenfranchised most Black citizens and many poor whites, a departure from the 1868 Reconstruction Constitution designed to prevent the majority Black population from voting. The poll tax, property requirements, and literacy tests also excluded poor whites, enabling Democrats to secure power and end the Republican challenge. From 1890 to 1908, such laws and constitutions were passed across the South, creating a one-party Democratic South. This period, known as the Solid South, disenfranchised large portions of the population, severely limiting the influence of the South Carolina Republican Party for generations. This control lasted until the second half of the 20th century. In the 1960s, the Civil Rights Movement intensified, and on July 1, 1964, the Civil Rights Act was passed with support from Democratic President Lyndon B. Johnson, ending legal segregation in public accommodations. On September 16, 1964, Senator Strom Thurmond announced he had switched from the Democratic Party to the Republican Party, stating the Democratic "party of our fathers is dead," claiming it had "forsaken the people to become the party of minority groups, power-hungry union leaders, political bosses, and businessmen looking for government contracts and favors." The Voting Rights Act of 1965 followed, restoring voting rights to minorities through federal oversight. In 1967, Carolyn Frederick was elected to represent House District 22 in Greenville County, becoming the first Republican woman elected to the South Carolina House. In 1974, James B. Edwards became the first Republican elected governor of South Carolina since Reconstruction. Since the late 20th century, South Carolina voters have increasingly supported Republican candidates for local, state, and national offices. In 2010, Republican Mick Mulvaney was elected to represent South Carolina's 5th congressional district, the first Republican to hold that seat since Robert Smalls, the party's co-founder, last held it in 1883; this marked the first break in over 100 years of Democratic control in the state legislature. Also in 2010, Republican Nikki Haley was elected the first female governor of South Carolina and the second Indian-American, after Bobby Jindal, to serve as a U.S. governor. South Carolina's January 21, 2012 Republican Presidential Preference Primary was the party's largest ever, drawing over 600,000 voters; Newt Gingrich won with 40.4% of the vote. The election set multiple state records, with five presidential debates and $13.2 million spent on television ads. Governor Haley appointed Tim Scott to the U.S. Senate; Scott is the first African-American senator from South Carolina and the first from the South since 1881. In the February 20, 2016 Republican Presidential Preference Primary, over 740,000 voters participated, setting a new turnout record; Donald Trump won with 32.5% of the vote. As President Donald Trump faced no significant primary opposition, the SCGOP canceled the 2020 Republican Presidential Preference Primary. In the 2024 Republican primary election, President Trump received the most votes in the history of the state's primaries. The party is led by an elected group of state party officers, the South Carolina Republican Party State Executive Committee, and paid staff, with its headquarters in Columbia, South Carolina. Republicans also hold both U.S. Senate seats and six of the seven U.S. House of Representatives seats. In 2012, Republican Tom Rice became the representative of South Carolina's 7th congressional district, newly re-established due to population gains; he is the first person to represent that district since it was eliminated in 1933. In a 2013 special election, former Republican Governor Mark Sanford was elected to represent South Carolina's 1st congressional district, returning to the seat he previously held from 1995 to 2001.
